comments.text:
Fun fact about giant spiders:
Real spiders move using hydraulic pressure in their legs, not big muscles. That works great when they’re tiny, but if a spider were scaled up to human-hunting size, its weight would increase way faster than its leg strength. The exoskeleton would be too heavy, the hydraulics wouldn’t generate enough force, and its breathing system couldn’t supply enough oxygen.

So instead of sprinting like in Huntsman, a real giant spider would actually be slow, struggling to even lift itself. The “25 m/s giant Huntsman speed” people quote online is just math that ignores biology — fun for games, but physically impossible in real life.

comments.text:
The reason spiders have "dump trucks" is because that is where almost all their vital organs are located. If that abdomen gets ruptured at all, it pretty much means game over for that spider. It's why many spider enthusiasts hardly pick up their spiders. If they fall and rupture that abdomen, there goes that spider.

Also what is interesting is this huntsman made a web, which is actually very atypical. Damn near unheard of for them actually. They hunt by ambush and camouflage and rushing down their prey when they get too close.

The giant huntsman spider (Heteropoda maxima) is a remarkable cave-dwelling arachnid distinguished by its extraordinary leg span, which can extend up to 30 centimeters (approximately 12 inches), making it the largest known spider species by this measure. First formally described in 2001 by German arachnologist Peter Jäger, this species was discovered in a remote cave in Laos, an environment that provides essential adaptations for its survival. The giant huntsman exhibits a high degree of agility and speed, facilitated by its elongated legs, which enable it to navigate its subterranean habitat adeptly. 

Notably, despite its imposing size and formidable appearance, the giant huntsman spider poses no threat to humans; it is generally regarded as non-venomous and harmless. The discovery of this species has contributed significantly to the understanding of biodiversity within cave ecosystems and underscores the ecological importance of such unique organisms in their respective environments.
